Predictive Modeling with Linear Regression
Project

Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

An over-the-top (OTT) media service is a media service offered directly to viewers via the internet. The term is most synonymous with subscription-based video-on-demand services that offer access to film and television content, including existing series acquired from other producers, as well as original content produced specifically for the service. They are typically accessed via websites on personal computers, apps on smartphones and tablets, or televisions with integrated Smart TV platforms.

Presently, OTT services are at a relatively nascent stage and are widely accepted as a trending technology across the globe. With the increasing change in customers' social behavior, which is shifting from traditional subscriptions to broadcasting services and OTT on-demand video and music subscriptions every year, OTT streaming is expected to grow at a very fast pace. The global OTT market size was valued at $121.61 billion in 2019 and is projected to reach $1,039.03 billion by 2027, growing at a CAGR of 29.4% from 2020 to 2027. The shift from television to OTT services for entertainment is driven by benefits such as on-demand services, ease of access, and access to better networks and digital connectivity.

With the outbreak of COVID-19, OTT services are striving to meet the growing entertainment appetite of viewers, with some platforms already experiencing a 46% increase in consumption and subscriber count as viewers seek fresh content. With innovations and advanced transformations, which will enable the customers to access everything they want in a single space, OTT platforms across the world are expected to increasingly attract subscribers on a concurrent basis.

Objective¶

ShowTime is an OTT service provider and offers a wide variety of content (movies, web shows, etc.) for its users. They want to determine the driver variables for first-day content viewership so that they can take necessary measures to improve the viewership of the content on their platform. Some of the reasons for the decline in viewership of content would be the decline in the number of people coming to the platform, decreased marketing spend, content timing clashes, weekends and holidays, etc. They have hired you as a Data Scientist, shared the data of the current content on their platform, and asked you to analyze the data and come up with a linear regression model to determine the driving factors for first-day viewership.

Data Dictionary¶

  • Visitors: Average number of visitors, in millions, to the platform in the past week
  • Ad_Impressions: Number of ad impressions, in millions, across all ad campaigns for the content (running and completed)
  • Major_Sports_Event: Any major sports event on the day
  • Genre: Genre of the content
  • Dayofweek: Day of the release of the content
  • Season: Season of the release of the content
  • Views_trailer: Number of views, in millions, of the content trailer
  • Views_content: Number of first-day views, in millions, of the content

Answers to Key Business Questions¶

1. What does the distribution of content views look like?

  • The distribution of first-day content views is approximately normal with moderate variability.
  • Most content receives average to moderate levels of first-day viewership, while only a small number of content releases achieve exceptionally high viewership.
  • The distribution indicates that content performance varies considerably across releases, suggesting that multiple factors influence audience engagement.

2. What does the distribution of genres look like?

  • Content is distributed across multiple genres, including Action, Comedy, Drama, Horror, Romance, Sci-Fi, Thriller, and Others.
  • The genre distribution is relatively balanced, ensuring fair representation of different content categories.
  • The "Others" category contains the highest number of content releases, while the remaining genres have comparable frequencies.

3. How does viewership vary with the day of release?

  • First-day content viewership varies noticeably across different release days.
  • Content released on certain days (like Friday and Wednesday) tends to achieve higher median viewership, indicating that audience engagement is influenced by release timing.
  • Strategically selecting the release day can help maximize first-day content consumption.

4. How does viewership vary with the season of release?

  • Content viewership exhibits moderate variation across different seasons.
  • Seasonal differences (with Summer and Winter performing strongly) demonstrate that audience availability and holidays contribute to content performance.

5. What is the correlation between trailer views and content views?

  • Trailer views exhibit the strongest positive relationship with first-day content views (correlation coefficient ≈ 0.75).
  • Content that generates higher trailer engagement before release tends to attract significantly more viewers on the first day.
  • This suggests that trailer popularity is one of the most important drivers of content performance.

Additional Insights from EDA

  • Platform visitors show a positive relationship with first-day content views, indicating that higher platform traffic contributes to increased content consumption.
  • Major sports events negatively impact content viewership, suggesting that audience attention shifts toward live sporting events during such occasions.
  • Ad impressions display a relatively weak direct relationship with content views, indicating that marketing exposure alone may not guarantee higher viewership.
  • Genre, release timing, and seasonal factors also contribute to differences in content performance and should be considered when planning future content releases.

Generate Predictions and Evaluate Performance (R²)¶

Build OLS Model for Interpretation¶

Using statsmodels to identify driver variables through p-values and coefficients.

In [43]:
# Adding a constant for the intercept term
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train)

# Converting to float to avoid object-type/boolean errors in statsmodels
X_train_sm = X_train_sm.astype(float)
y_train = y_train.astype(float)

# Fitting the OLS model
ols_model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()

print(ols_model.summary())

Linear Regression Assumptions¶

Multicollinearity Check (VIF)¶

We check if independent variables are highly correlated with each other using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF).

In [47]:
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

# Create a dataframe for VIF
vif = pd.DataFrame()
vif["Feature"] = X_train.columns
vif["VIF"] = [
    variance_inflation_factor(X_train.astype(float).values, i)
    for i in range(X_train.shape[1])
]

display(vif.sort_values("VIF", ascending=False))

Observations on Multicollinearity:

  • The features visitors (VIF ≈ 24.5) and ad_impressions (VIF ≈ 20.3) exhibit high multicollinearity, exceeding the standard threshold of 10.
  • This suggests that platform traffic and advertising efforts are closely linked, which might make it difficult for the model to isolate their individual impacts accurately.
  • Most other variables, including genre and seasonal dummies, show VIF values below 5, indicating they are relatively independent predictors.

Residual Normality¶

Residuals should follow an approximately normal distribution for valid statistical inference.

In [48]:
# Residuals were previously defined but let's ensure they match the OLS model
y_train_pred = ols_model.predict(X_train_sm)
residuals = y_train - y_train_pred

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

# Histogram
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
sns.histplot(residuals, kde=True)
plt.title("Distribution of Residuals")

# QQ Plot
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
sm.qqplot(residuals, line='45', fit=True, ax=plt.gca())
plt.title("Q-Q Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations on Residual Normality:

  • The histogram of residuals follows a distinct bell-shaped curve centered at zero, suggesting that errors are symmetrically distributed.
  • The Q-Q Plot shows that most residuals lie directly on the 45-degree reference line, with only slight deviations at the extreme ends of the distribution.
  • Conclusion: The assumption of normality is satisfied, ensuring that our p-values and confidence intervals for the model coefficients are reliable.

Homoscedasticity and Linearity¶

We check for constant variance (homoscedasticity) and a linear relationship between actual and predicted values.

In [49]:
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

# Residual vs Predicted (Homoscedasticity)
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
sns.scatterplot(x=y_train_pred, y=residuals)
plt.axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Predicted Values")
plt.ylabel("Residuals")
plt.title("Residuals vs Predicted")

# Actual vs Predicted (Linearity)
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
sns.scatterplot(x=y_train_pred, y=y_train)
plt.plot([y_train.min(), y_train.max()], [y_train.min(), y_train.max()], color='red', lw=2)
plt.xlabel("Predicted Values")
plt.ylabel("Actual Values")
plt.title("Actual vs Predicted")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations on Homoscedasticity and Linearity:

  • Homoscedasticity: In the 'Residuals vs Predicted' plot, the data points are randomly dispersed around the horizontal axis without forming any specific pattern (like a wedge or funnel). This indicates constant variance in the error terms.
  • Linearity: The 'Actual vs Predicted' plot shows a strong diagonal alignment. The points follow the identity line closely, confirming that the relationship between the predictors and first-day viewership is inherently linear.

Independence of Errors¶

We use the Durbin-Watson test to check for autocorrelation in residuals (values near 2.0 indicate independence).

In [50]:
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
dw_score = durbin_watson(residuals)
print(f"Durbin-Watson score: {dw_score:.4f}")

Durbin-Watson score: 2.0258

Observations on Independence of Errors:

  • The calculated Durbin-Watson score of 2.026 is very close to the ideal value of 2.0.
  • This indicates that there is no significant autocorrelation present in the residuals, meaning each observation's error is independent of the others.

Final Model Refinement¶

In this step, we drop the variables that were statistically insignificant (p-value > 0.05) in the initial OLS model to create a more robust and interpretable model.

Variables to be dropped:

  • ad_impressions (p=0.257)
  • genre_Comedy (p=0.167)
  • genre_Others (p=0.281)
  • genre_Romance (p=0.909)
  • dayofweek_Tuesday (p=0.110)
In [54]:
# Identifying all variables with p-value > 0.05 from the previous output
# This includes the initial list plus remaining genres and Thursday
final_cols_to_drop = [
    'ad_impressions', 'genre_Comedy', 'genre_Others', 'genre_Romance',
    'dayofweek_Tuesday', 'genre_Drama', 'genre_Horror', 'genre_Sci-Fi',
    'genre_Thriller', 'dayofweek_Thursday'
]

# Prepare refined feature sets
X_train_v2 = X_train.drop(columns=final_cols_to_drop)
X_test_v2 = X_test.drop(columns=final_cols_to_drop)

# Build Re-Refined OLS Model
X_train_v2_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train_v2).astype(float)
final_ols_model_v2 = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_v2_sm).fit()

Model Comparison: Initial vs Final¶

We will now compare the performance of the initial model (all variables) against the final model (significant variables only) using Adjusted R² and RMSE.

In [55]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

print(f"Final Model (Strict p < 0.05) Adjusted R2: {final_ols_model_v2.rsquared_adj:.4f}")

# RMSE Comparison
initial_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, ols_model.predict(X_train_sm)))
final_rmse_v2 = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, final_ols_model_v2.predict(X_train_v2_sm)))

print(f"Final Model RMSE: {final_rmse_v2:.4f}")

# Test Set Performance
X_test_v2_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test_v2).astype(float)
test_rmse_v2 = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, final_ols_model_v2.predict(X_test_v2_sm)))
print(f"Final Model Test RMSE: {test_rmse_v2:.4f}")

Final Model Summary and Observation¶

  • Variable Selection: We removed ad_impressions, genre_Comedy, genre_Others, genre_Romance, and dayofweek_Tuesday as they were statistically insignificant.
  • Performance Stability: The Adjusted R² only dropped by a negligible amount (from ~0.780 to ~0.779), and the RMSE remained virtually identical.
  • Parsimony: The final model is preferred as it achieves the same explanatory power with fewer variables, reducing the risk of overfitting and making it easier for the business to focus on the key drivers: Visitors, Trailer Views, Major Sports Events, and Seasonality.
In [56]:

Final Model Adjusted R-squared: 0.7780

Final Model Interpretation and Comparison¶

  • Adjusted R²: Check if the Adjusted R-squared remained stable (around 0.78). If it didn't drop significantly, the removed variables were indeed redundant.
  • Significant Drivers:
    • Visitors & Trailer Views: Remain the strongest positive drivers.
    • Major Sports Event: Confirmed as a significant negative driver.
    • Seasonality: All seasons (Summer, Winter, Spring) show significant positive coefficients relative to the baseline (Fall).

Insights & Recommendations¶

This section outlines the key business takeaways derived from the final regression model. All findings are focused on actionable strategies to improve first-day content viewership.

Key Insights¶

  1. Trailer Views are the Strongest Driver

    • Insight: Trailer engagement is the single most reliable predictor of success. High trailer viewership creates a strong launch-day pull.
    • Recommendation: Prioritize the production and organic reach of trailers. Use trailer engagement metrics as an early warning system to adjust marketing spend before the actual content launch.

  2. Platform Traffic Directly Influences Viewership

    • Insight: There is a direct positive correlation between the number of weekly visitors to the platform and the viewership of new releases.
    • Recommendation: Launch high-value content during weeks where overall platform traffic is expected to be high. Use cross-promotion and app notifications to boost general platform visits in the days leading up to a major release.

  3. Major Sports Events Negatively Impact Viewership

    • Insight: Releasing content during major sporting events leads to a significant reduction in first-day views due to audience diversion.
    • Recommendation: Avoid scheduling 'Flagship' or 'Premium' content releases on days that clash with major international or local sporting finals.

  4. Release Timing Matters (Day and Season)

    • Insight: Performance varies by day. Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday are historically strong release windows for ShowTime. Seasonally, Summer releases perform significantly better than Fall.
    • Recommendation: Align major releases with the Summer season and weekend windows to capitalize on increased user leisure time.

  5. Advertising Volume vs. Efficiency

    • Insight: General 'Ad Impressions' did not show a statistically significant impact on first-day views when compared to organic trailer engagement.
    • Recommendation: Shift the marketing budget from high-volume, low-intent ad impressions toward high-quality trailer placements and content discovery features within the platform.

Business Recommendations¶

  • Short-Term: Optimize the immediate release calendar by moving upcoming releases away from sports conflicts and onto Wednesdays or Saturdays.
  • Long-Term: Develop a 'Trailer-First' marketing strategy where the success of a trailer determines the level of promotional support the final content receives.

Conclusion¶

The objective of this project was to identify the key factors influencing first-day content viewership on the ShowTime OTT platform and develop a linear regression model capable of predicting content performance.

A comprehensive exploratory data analysis was conducted to understand the characteristics of the dataset and the relationships between the predictor variables and first-day content views. The analysis revealed that trailer engagement, platform visitor traffic, release timing, and major sports events have a notable impact on content viewership. In particular, content with higher trailer views tended to attract significantly larger audiences on the day of release, while major sports events were found to negatively affect viewership by competing for audience attention.

Multiple Linear Regression was used to model first-day content views. After evaluating the initial model and testing the assumptions of linear regression, statistically insignificant variables were removed to create a more interpretable final model. The final model maintained performance comparable to the initial model, with only a negligible decrease in Adjusted R² and a very small increase in RMSE, indicating that the removed variables contributed limited additional explanatory power.

Overall, the final model successfully identified the primary drivers of content viewership and can serve as a valuable decision-support tool for ShowTime. The findings suggest that increasing trailer engagement, maximizing platform traffic before releases, strategically scheduling content launches, and avoiding clashes with major sports events can significantly improve first-day content performance. These insights can help ShowTime optimize its marketing strategies, content release planning, and resource allocation to maximize audience engagement and viewership growth.
